conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here at the clinic, and I specialize in supporting new mothers in the weeks and months after delivery.  

I’m going to ask you ten brief questions from what we call the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. This is simply a standard way we check in on how moms are feeling emotionally—especially because the postpartum period can bring mood changes that are easy to brush aside when you’re focused on your baby. Your answers are completely confidential; they help me understand what kind of support or resources might be helpful for you right now. There are no right or wrong responses, and you can take your time.

We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about exact numbers or labels. When we’re done, I’ll add up the responses and we can talk about next steps together.  

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:  

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I can still laugh sometimes—like the other day my husband made a silly face and it surprised a laugh out of me—but most of the time it feels forced, like I’m too tired or heavy inside to really find things funny the way I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not very often. I laughed once or twice when my husband joked around, but it felt kind of flat, like I had to work for it. Most of the week nothing really struck me as funny—I’m just too worn-out and low.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks—like I was sort of excited to take the baby for a walk yesterday—but mostly I don’t look forward to much. Even things I used to love feel kind of “meh,” and I catch myself thinking “what’s the point?” before I do them.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong or I’m not soothing him right. I keep replaying little moments—like when I couldn’t get him to latch quickly—and I tell myself I’m failing him. I know in my head it’s probably not true, but the guilty thoughts just keep coming.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly picture him choking or getting sick, and then I can’t shake the worry even after I check him and he’s fine. Sometimes I’m just staring at the monitor at night, heart racing, waiting for something bad to happen that never does.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week—like yesterday when I was folding laundry—my chest got tight and my heart started racing out of nowhere. I kept thinking something awful was about to happen to the baby, even though everything was quiet and he was asleep. It lasted maybe ten minutes before I could breathe normally again.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—most days feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t nap unless I held him, dishes piled up, and I just stood in the kitchen crying because it felt like too much. I get through it, but it’s like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” about the baby. Most nights this week I couldn’t fall asleep for at least an hour, and when I do drift off I wake up suddenly, heart pounding, sure I heard him cry—even if he’s still asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s not tears-all-day awful, but there’s this heavy sadness that hangs over everything. Even when I’m holding the baby and he’s smiling, I feel like I’m watching it through a gray fog.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Twice this week—once in the shower where no one could see, and once when my mom asked how I was doing. The tears just came out of nowhere and I couldn’t stop them, even though I hate crying in front of people.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It has crossed my mind a couple of times—like a quick flash of “what if I just wasn’t here?”—but I’ve never planned anything and I don’t want to leave the baby. They’re more like scared, passing thoughts when everything feels too heavy.

You've shared that over the past week most days feel heavy and gray: you rarely laugh, daily worries about the baby race through your mind, and you often feel overwhelmed, tearful, and guilty. You expressed <quote>little sparks</quote> of enjoyment but quickly return to feeling sad, exhausted, and <quote>like I'm failing him</quote>. Sleep is broken by anxious thoughts, and you've had brief, scary flashes of wishing you weren't here, though you emphasize you don't want to leave your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughing only once or twice and describes the laughter as forced and lacking genuine enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports only rare sparks of enjoyment and frequent "what's the point?" thinking, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses frequent self-blame ('a lot'), rumination over minor incidents, and persistent guilt despite insight, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries about infant safety that persist despite reassurance—clearly matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic symptoms (tight chest, racing heart, dread) without an external trigger—clearly maps to "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days" and "drowning in small stuff," unable to cope and reduced to tears, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly sleep difficulty linked to anxious thoughts and intrusive worries, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness that colors all experiences, matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total ≥14 indicates probable major depression; your score of 24 is well above that threshold. You endorse core symptoms of <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest, excessive guilt, fatigue, insomnia, and recurrent thoughts of death. Co-occurring <med>anxiety symptoms</med> and panic-like episodes are common in postpartum depression. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist for full evaluation
2. Develop a written safety plan with supports and 24-hour crisis contacts; monitor Q10 score ≥1 immediately
3. Schedule brief therapy or support group within one week; evidence-based options include CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression
4. Involve a trusted adult for practical help at home; encourage short daily rest periods and nutritious snacks
5. Practice 5-minute grounding or breathing exercises when panic symptoms arise; keep baby nearby for reassurance
6. Re-screen EPDS in two weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen or active suicidal thoughts emerge
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant approx. ≤3 months  
Date: [today]

1. Primary endorsed symptoms  
   – Persistent low mood, anhedonia, “gray fog” (Q1, Q2, Q8)  
   – Daily tearfulness, easily triggered crying (Q9)  
   – Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia tied to ruminative worry (Q7)  
   – Excessive guilt/self-blame re parenting competence (Q3)  
   – Recurrent intrusive fears of infant harm, no objective basis (Q4, Q5)  
   – Episodic physiological panic (tight chest, racing heart) without precipitant (Q5)  
   – Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning,” difficulty completing routine tasks (Q6)

2. Pattern consistency  
   Symptoms cluster: mood, anxiety, cognitive distortions, functional impairment, all present ≥ daily for past week.

3. Screening significance  
   Meets provisional cutoff for probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety features; rule-out postpartum anxiety disorder.

4. Safety flag  
   Passive self-harm ideation (“what if I just wasn’t here?”) reported; no plan, intent, or active desire to die. Immediate protective factors: strong infant attachment, supportive spouse and mother.

5. Risk factors  
   – Daily sadness, anhedonia, guilt  
   – Insomnia secondary to mood  
   – Spontaneous panic symptoms  
   – Passive suicidal cognitions → requires formal safety assessment

6. Next screening steps (documented for referral)  
   – Administer EPDS for quantitative score  
   – Same-day safety plan review (means, supports, 24-h contacts)  
   – Expedited referral to perinatal psychiatry / therapist team  
   – Consider lab work to rule-out organic contributors (thyroid, anemia)

End of screening note
